title: The Annual Wealth Review: One Day That Audits the Whole Architecture
summary: This checkpoint week rehearses an annual wealth review, the one meeting a year that tests every layer of your personal architecture at once. Warrick revisits the phase's hardest ideas: ownership layers, liquidity tiers, currency reserves, position sizing and the cost of advice.
body:
An annual wealth review is not a performance report. It is an inspection of the structure: who owns what, how much can be reached in a crisis, how much rides on one bet, what it all costs, and who takes over if you cannot. Done once a year, properly, it catches most of the failures we studied last week while they are still cheap.

Recall

Q. What three things does a bridge from opening to closing equity separate?

A. At minimum, the market price effect, the currency effect and the effect of debt repayment, with fees, income and tax added in a full version. Each line is tagged as a market outcome or a design choice.

Q. Why is the timing of retirement withdrawals a tax question as well as a spending question?

A. Because different accounts are taxed differently on withdrawal, so the order changes the after-tax income from the same assets. Verify the rules against the primary source before you rely on them.

Q. Why does timing matter in asset protection?

A. Because transfers made when a claim is foreseeable, or that leave you unable to pay known debts, can be challenged and reversed. Protection put in place early, for genuine reasons, is far more robust than protection put in place under pressure.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this is a checkpoint week. For eleven weeks we built the architecture of your personal wealth, one layer at a time. This week we use it, the way a real annual review would. A structure that is never inspected drifts: positions grow, currencies move, documents age, advisers change. The annual review is the inspection, and like a building inspection, its value is in what it finds before anything fails.

The five layers the review walks through

First, ownership layers. In week 85 we separated the layers: operating companies that carry project risk, holding companies that receive profits, and personal and family assets that should be insulated from both. The review asks whether anything has drifted into the wrong layer. A typical drift is a personal asset quietly pledged to a project lender, which moves it from the safe layer to the risky one.

Second, liquidity tiers. Tier 1 is cash you can use today. Tier 2 is assets you can turn to cash in weeks without a large loss. Tier 3 is everything else, including your development equity. The review checks that tiers 1 and 2 together still cover your written floor, in the currency of your obligations.

Third, position sizing and concentration. In week 86, Warrick and Roman set a maximum share for any single exposure. The review compares today's shares with those limits, and treats a breach as a decision to make now, not a note for next year.

Fourth, cost and conflicts. In week 87 we saw that fees compound like returns, in reverse, and that every adviser has incentives. The review totals what you paid everyone, as a share of the assets they touch, and asks whether each relationship still earns its place.

Fifth, protection and succession. Insurance, wills, powers of attorney, trusts and company signing authorities. The review checks that each still matches the balance sheet you just built.

Say that out loud now.

The annual review inspects the structure, not the returns. Ownership, liquidity, concentration, cost and succession.

Worked example one: the drift you only see once a year

All numbers are hypothetical. Last year a developer's personal balance sheet showed 8,000,000 dollars of net worth, with his largest single project at 40 percent of total assets, under a written limit of 50 percent. During the year the project was revalued upward and he reinvested a distribution into it. This year it stands at 58 percent. Nothing was wrong with either decision on its own. Together they breached the limit, and nobody noticed until the review placed this year's figure beside last year's limit.

The review's job is to record the breach and choose one of three responses: reduce the exposure, raise the limit with a written reason, or accept the breach for a defined period with a written plan to cure it. Doing nothing is not one of the options.

Worked example two: the reserve in the wrong currency

Second hypothetical. Liquidity tier 1 holds 600,000 units of currency F. The developer's living costs and his largest guarantee are in currency H. His written floor is 500,000 H. At last year's rate of 1 F to 1 H, the floor was covered. This year the rate is 1 F to 0.75 H, so the same reserve is worth 450,000 H, below the floor. The review catches it because it measures the reserve in the currency of the obligation, not in the currency it happens to be held in.

Worked example three: the fees nobody added up

Third hypothetical. The developer has an investment account of 2,000,000 dollars with a manager charging 1 percent a year, which is 20,000 dollars. The manager places part of it in funds that charge their own 1 percent on 1,000,000 dollars, another 10,000. A bank charges 3,000 dollars a year in account and transfer fees, an accountant 12,000 and a lawyer 15,000 for routine work. No single bill looks large. The total is 60,000 dollars a year, which is 3 percent of the 2,000,000 dollar account, and every dollar of it comes off the return before compounding.

The review does not say any of those fees is wrong. It puts them on one line, beside the value each relationship delivered, so that you can decide which to keep with your eyes open. Fees are commercial terms, not standards; whether a fee is fair depends on the work and on what the market charges for it.

How the best do it

Well-run family offices tend to treat the annual review as a formal meeting with a fixed agenda, papers circulated in advance, minutes and a list of decisions with owners and dates. The papers usually include a consolidated statement in one currency, a table of every limit against its current value, and a summary of estate and insurance documents with their review dates. A small developer can copy all of it with a spreadsheet, a one-page agenda and two hours of honest attention.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is turning the review into a celebration of returns. A strong year makes everyone relaxed, and the structural questions get skipped. The control is the agenda: structure first, returns last, and no item closed without a decision recorded.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner reviews each account with the adviser who runs it, one at a time. Nobody sees the whole picture, so concentration, currency exposure and duplicated fees hide in the gaps between statements. Always review the consolidated view first, then the parts.

Omar's Six-Lens Check

Tax: the review should note each tax deadline and each structure whose tax treatment may have changed, and verify it against the primary source before you rely on it. Liability: check that no personal asset has drifted into a layer exposed to project creditors. Banking: confirm at least two working banking relationships and current signing authorities. Governance: record who decided what, and who may act if you cannot. Estate: match every document to this year's balance sheet. Exit: for each large position, write down how and how fast it could be sold if it had to be.

Callback

In week 48, Marco taught the owner's decision log for a project: every material decision recorded with its reason and its owner. The annual wealth review is the decision log for your family's balance sheet. A year from now, you will want to know not only what you decided, but why, and what you knew at the time.

Recap

The annual review inspects five layers: ownership, liquidity, concentration, cost and succession. It measures everything in the currency of your obligations, compares every figure with a written limit, and closes no item without a decision.

Next: Ford, with Cole assisting, on Failure Forensics: the Howard Hughes estate and the price of having no current plan.
checklist: I hold one annual wealth review with a written agenda.
Structure comes before returns on that agenda.
I review a consolidated statement in one reporting currency first.
I compare every position with its written limit.
I measure liquidity in the currency of my obligations.
I total all fees paid as a share of the assets each adviser touches.
I match every estate and insurance document to this year's balance sheet.
I close no item without a recorded decision, owner and date.
head: Field checklist
speak: Mr Shabazz, an annual wealth review inspects the structure, not the returns. It walks five layers. Ownership: has anything drifted into a layer exposed to project creditors? Liquidity: do tiers 1 and 2 still cover the written floor, measured in the currency of my obligations? Concentration: does any position now exceed its written limit, perhaps because it was revalued or I reinvested into it? Cost: what did I pay every adviser, and does each still earn its place? And succession: do my wills, powers of attorney, insurance and company signing authorities match this year's balance sheet? Every breach gets one of three answers: reduce it, raise the limit with a written reason, or accept it for a defined period with a plan. Doing nothing is not an option. The best family offices run this as a formal meeting with papers, minutes and dated decisions. A licensed adviser is required before I act.
terms: Annual wealth review — a yearly formal inspection of the whole personal balance sheet against written limits and documents.
Liquidity tier — a band of assets grouped by how quickly they can become usable cash without a large loss.
Ownership layer — a level of the structure, such as operating company, holding company or personal assets, separated to contain risk.

hostile.q: Your largest project is now well above your own written concentration limit. Why should I believe your limits mean anything?
hostile.a: Because the review caught it and I recorded a decision. The breach came from an upward revaluation plus a reinvested distribution, and I have chosen to cure it within a stated period by directing future distributions elsewhere and not committing new equity to that project. If it is not cured by that date, the written fallback is a partial sale. The limit is enforced by the review, not by memory.

role: Failure forensics, with Cole (Audit and integrity)
title: The Hughes Estate: A Great Fortune With No Current Plan
summary: Howard Hughes died in April 1976 with one of the largest fortunes of his time and no valid will that anyone could find. Purported wills surfaced, courts spent years sorting heirs and domicile, and control of his businesses had already passed to others during his decline. We take it through seven steps and end with the rule that closes every annual review.
body:
Howard Hughes was famous for control, and he died without the one document that would have controlled what happened next. The failure was not a lack of money or advisers. It was the absence of a current, findable plan, reviewed while he could still sign it.

Recall

Q. In the currency-loss bridge from last week, which effect was the design choice?

A. The currency effect on the borrowed part. Borrowing in the home currency against a foreign asset exposed the whole asset value to the exchange rate, and a matched loan would have saved most of the loss.

Q. Why does the mix of salary and dividends matter to someone who owns a company?

A. Because the two are taxed differently in the company and in the owner's hands, and each affects entitlements and the company's retained cash differently. The right mix depends on local rules; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

Q. What is a fraudulent or voidable transfer, in concept?

A. A transfer of assets that a court can reverse because it was made to defeat creditors or left the transferor unable to pay known debts. The tests and time limits vary by jurisdiction.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Cole joins me because this is an estate case and a governance case at once. Hughes did not lack talent, money or lawyers. He lacked a plan that existed in a form a court would accept, and in his last years he lacked the capacity to supervise those who ran his affairs. A developer with complex holdings faces the same two risks on a smaller scale.

The broad facts are drawn from the public record. Where I am unsure of a detail I say so or leave out the number.

1. Timeline

Hughes built a fortune across aviation, film, tools and other businesses. In 1953 he founded the Howard Hughes Medical Institute. In his later years he lived in seclusion, in declining health, with a small group of aides controlling access to him. He died on April 5, 1976, on an aircraft carrying him to Houston for medical care. No valid will was found. Many documents claiming to be his will appeared. The best known, which became known as the Mormon Will, surfaced in 1976 and named among its beneficiaries a man who said he had once helped Hughes on a Nevada road. In 1978 a Nevada jury found it was not genuine. Courts then had to determine his legal heirs, and distant relatives eventually shared the estate. More than one state sought to treat him as domiciled there for estate tax purposes [unverified — confirm independently].

2. Key decisions

Three decisions, or failures to decide, mattered. Not executing a will, or not keeping one where it could be found and proved. Not putting in place a clear, supervised arrangement for decisions if he could no longer make them. And allowing an increasingly small circle of people to control both access to him and the running of his businesses.

3. Assumptions

The likely assumptions are familiar. That there would be time later. That intentions he had spoken about would somehow be honoured. That the people around him would act as he would have wished. And, for a man used to control, perhaps that discussing death and incapacity was unnecessary. Each assumption is common among founders, because the founder's identity is built on being the one who decides.

4. Incentives

Once a fortune has no valid will, many parties have an incentive to produce one, to contest one or to claim to be an heir. People around a declining founder may also have incentives that differ from his, simply because their positions depend on the arrangement continuing. No one needs to be dishonest for this to go wrong. The structure creates the pressure.

Say that out loud now.

If I leave no findable plan, I create an incentive for others to write one for me.

5. Warning signs ignored

Declining health. Increasing isolation. Decisions channelled through a few people. Public statements about intentions with no document behind them. In a developer's life, the equivalents are a founder who is the only signatory, who keeps documents in his head or in a drawer only he knows, and who postpones the estate meeting each year because a deal is closing.

6. Point of no return

The point of no return is the loss of capacity, not death. While Hughes could still understand and sign, a will, a power of attorney and a supervised governance arrangement were all possible. Once capacity had gone, they were not, and every question that followed had to be answered by courts and by whoever held the practical control.

7. Root cause

The root cause was treating the estate plan as a one-time intention rather than a maintained document. A plan that is not written, current, findable and consistent with the actual holdings is, for legal purposes, no plan.

Cole's view: auditing an estate plan

Cole reads an estate plan the way he reads a set of accounts. Is there a signed original? Where is it, and who knows? Does it describe the assets that exist today? Does it name people who are still alive, available and willing? Does a power of attorney cover the period before death? Does each company's own signing authority allow someone else to act?

A worked example, hypothetical. A developer's will, signed eight years ago, leaves his shares in a holding company to two named people and appoints an executor. Since then he has sold that holding company, formed three new project companies, moved assets into a second country and divorced. Cole's audit finds the will disposes of an asset that no longer exists, says nothing about the three companies, names an executor who has emigrated, and may be affected by the change in marriage, depending on local law. On paper there is a will. In substance, much of the estate would pass under default rules. The fix is a review, not a new idea.

A second example, on the cost of delay. Suppose updating the documents costs a few thousand dollars in legal fees and an afternoon. Against that, a contested or intestate administration of a hypothetical 10,000,000 dollar estate could take years and consume a material share of the estate in fees, delay and forced sales, while the family has no clear authority. The comparison is not close, which is why delay is a behavioural failure, not a financial one.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is that capacity goes before the plan is updated. The control is to tie the estate check to the annual wealth review, so that the review cannot be closed without it. Professional sign-off required: estate lawyer in each jurisdiction where assets are held.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner thinks he has a plan because he once signed a will. Plans decay with every sale, purchase, marriage, divorce, birth, death and move. The second mistake is telling no one where the original is. A will that cannot be found may be treated as if it does not exist.

Callback

Last week, in lesson 669, Tessa explained what the law does when there is no plan: default heirs, a court-appointed administrator, and a gap in authority during incapacity. Hughes is that lesson at the largest scale. The defaults are not designed for a complex fortune, and they do not ask what you would have wanted.

The prevention rule

Rule 97: I never close an annual review until my will, powers of attorney and beneficiary designations have been checked against the balance sheet I just built, updated where needed, and the location of every original recorded.

Recap

Hughes died in 1976 with no valid, findable will, after years in which control of his affairs had narrowed to a few people. Purported wills, contests and heirship questions followed. The root cause was a plan treated as an intention rather than a maintained document.

Next: Warrick, on The Money: the numbers an annual wealth review produces, and what each one tells you.
checklist: My will is signed, current and describes the assets I hold today.
At least two trusted people know where the original documents are.
My executor and attorneys are alive, available and willing.
I hold powers of attorney that cover a period of incapacity.
Each company I control lets someone else sign if I cannot.
I review the estate documents as part of every annual wealth review.
I update documents after any sale, purchase, marriage, divorce, birth, death or move.
Professional sign-off from an estate lawyer in each jurisdiction is recorded.
head: Field checklist
speak: Mr Shabazz, Howard Hughes died in April 1976 with an enormous fortune and no valid will anyone could find. In his last years he lived in seclusion, in poor health, with a small group of aides controlling access and decisions. After his death many purported wills appeared; the best known was rejected by a Nevada jury in 1978, and courts had to work out his heirs. The point of no return was the loss of capacity, not death, because while he could sign, a will, powers of attorney and supervised governance were all possible. The root cause was treating the plan as an intention instead of a maintained document. A will signed years ago, describing assets you no longer own, is not a plan. So Rule 97: I never close an annual review until my will, powers of attorney and beneficiary designations are checked against this year's balance sheet and the originals' location is recorded.
terms: Testamentary capacity — the mental ability required by law to make a valid will.
Executor — the person a will appoints to collect the assets, pay the debts and distribute the estate.
Domicile — a person's permanent legal home, which can decide which place's laws and taxes apply to the estate.

hostile.q: You tell me your estate plan is in order. When was it last checked against your actual holdings, and who has the originals?
hostile.a: It was checked at my last annual review, on a date I can show you, against the balance sheet produced the same day. Two named people know where the originals are held, and my lawyer confirmed in writing which documents needed updating. The next check is fixed in my calendar as part of next year's review, and I update sooner after any major transaction or family change.

rule: Rule 97: I never close an annual review until my will, powers of attorney and beneficiary designations have been checked against the balance sheet I just built, updated where needed, and the location of every original recorded.

title: Six Numbers Every Annual Wealth Review Must Produce
summary: An annual review should end with six numbers on one page: net worth in the reporting currency, liquidity coverage, concentration, personal leverage including guarantees, net currency exposure and all-in cost. Each has a written limit, and each tells you something different about whether a bad year is survivable.
body:
Net worth is the least useful number on your balance sheet. The review earns its keep with five others beside it: how much you can reach, how much rides on one bet, how much you owe including what you have guaranteed, how much depends on one currency, and what the whole structure costs to run.

Recall

Q. In a meeting with a new manager, what is the first question?

A. Who is the custodian, and is it independent of the manager's firm? Custody questions come before any discussion of returns.

Q. Why can registered or tax-sheltered accounts change the order in which you should spend assets in retirement?

A. Because withdrawals from them may be taxed differently from withdrawals from ordinary accounts, so the sequence changes the after-tax result. Verify the rules against the primary source before you rely on them.

Q. What does ring-fencing mean in asset protection?

A. Holding a risky activity in its own entity, so that its creditors can reach only that entity's assets and not the owner's other holdings, provided the separation is real and respected.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a lender looking at you as a guarantor, an investor looking at you as a partner, and your own family looking at you as a provider will each ask a different question. One page with six numbers answers all three. If you produce it every year, you will see your own trends long before anyone else does.

The six numbers

1. Net worth in the reporting currency. Total assets less total debts, all converted into the currency you spend, on one date.

2. Liquidity coverage. Tier 1 and tier 2 assets, those you can turn to cash in weeks, divided by your written floor. The floor is your chosen months of spending plus a realistic allowance for guarantees being called. Above 1.0 means the floor is covered.

3. Concentration ratio. The largest single exposure divided by total assets, checked against your written limit. Run it by asset, by market and by counterparty.

4. Personal leverage, with and without guarantees. Debt divided by total assets, then debt plus guarantees divided by total assets. The second figure is the one lenders care about, because a guarantee is a debt that has not yet arrived.

5. Net currency exposure. For each currency, assets less debts in that currency, as a share of net worth. The share in currencies other than the one you spend is your open position.

6. All-in cost. Every fee paid to managers, funds, banks, accountants and lawyers in the year, as a share of the assets they serve.

Say that out loud now.

Net worth, liquidity coverage, concentration, leverage with guarantees, currency exposure and all-in cost. Six numbers, one page, every year.

Worked example one: building the page

All figures are hypothetical, in dollars, with one currency for simplicity. Assets: project company shares 5,000,000; a rental building 3,000,000; a home 1,000,000; an investment account 800,000; cash 200,000. Total assets 10,000,000. Debts: rental mortgage 1,500,000; home mortgage 500,000. Total debt 2,000,000. Guarantees on a construction loan: 3,000,000. Annual spending: 120,000. Written floor: 12 months of spending plus 20 percent of guarantees, which is 120,000 plus 600,000, or 720,000.

Net worth is 10,000,000 less 2,000,000, which is 8,000,000. Liquidity: cash 200,000 plus the investment account 800,000 is 1,000,000, divided by the 720,000 floor, which is about 1.39. Concentration: project shares of 5,000,000 divided by 10,000,000 is 50 percent. Leverage without guarantees: 2,000,000 divided by 10,000,000 is 20 percent. With guarantees: 5,000,000 divided by 10,000,000 is 50 percent. All-in cost: suppose fees of 40,000 on the 800,000 account and other advisory costs of 30,000, a total of 70,000. Against the 800,000 invested account alone that is 8.75 percent, which is a warning; against all assets it is 0.7 percent. Show both, because the first tells you whether the managed account is paying its way.

Worked example two: what the trend tells you

Now the same page a year later, hypothetical. Net worth has risen to 9,000,000, which feels like progress. But the project shares are now 6,500,000 of 11,000,000 total assets, 59 percent. Guarantees have risen to 5,000,000 because a second loan closed. Cash and investments are unchanged at 1,000,000. The floor is now 120,000 plus 20 percent of 5,000,000, which is 1,120,000. Liquidity coverage is 1,000,000 divided by 1,120,000, about 0.89. Below 1.0.

Net worth went up by 1,000,000 and the family became less safe. Concentration rose, contingent debt rose, and liquidity fell below the floor. Only the page side by side with last year's page shows it. The decision follows: fund the gap in the floor before the next guarantee is signed, or decline the next guarantee.

Worked example three: the currency line

Add currencies to the first example, still hypothetical. Suppose the project shares and the rental building, 8,000,000 of assets, are valued in currency F, and the rental mortgage of 1,500,000 is also in F. Everything else is in H, the currency the family spends. Net exposure to F is 8,000,000 less 1,500,000, which is 6,500,000, or about 81 percent of the 8,000,000 net worth. Only about 19 percent of net worth is in the currency of daily life.

Now test it. A 20 percent fall in F against H reduces the F position by 1,300,000 in H terms, so net worth falls to about 6,700,000. Nothing happened to the buildings. Whether 81 percent is acceptable is your decision, not a rule, but the page makes sure you decide it consciously. Note too where the liquidity sits: if the 1,000,000 of cash and investments were in F rather than H, the floor would fall with the currency as well, which is the beginner's error from week 96.

Warrick's Wealth Ledger

Warrick's ledger for this subject is the page itself, kept year by year in one file. Add one column for each number's written limit and one for the decision made when a limit is breached. Over five years, the file becomes the most honest description of how you actually manage risk, rather than how you think you do. A licensed adviser is required before you act on any of the decisions it prompts.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is leaving guarantees off the page because they are not on any statement. They are often the largest liability you carry. The control is a guarantee register, reconciled to the signed documents, that feeds numbers 2 and 4 every year.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner judges the year by number 1 alone. Net worth can rise while every other number gets worse, as the second example showed. Read the six together, and read them against last year.

Callback

In week 36, Priya taught sizing a loan to the binding constraint: whichever of debt service coverage, loan-to-value or debt yield bites first sets the loan. Your personal page works the same way. Whichever of the six numbers is closest to its limit is the binding constraint on your next commitment, and it is rarely net worth.

Decision journals

The six numbers tell you what your position is. They do not tell you why you chose it. Keep a short decision journal beside the page: for each material decision, write the date, what you decided, the numbers you looked at, what you expected to happen and what would prove you wrong. It takes five minutes and it is the only reliable defence against remembering your past reasoning as better than it was.

At the next annual review, read last year's entries before you read this year's numbers. You will learn more about your own judgment from that half hour than from any performance report.

Recap

The review produces six numbers on one page: net worth, liquidity coverage, concentration, leverage with guarantees, currency exposure and all-in cost, each beside its limit and last year's figure. Net worth can rise while safety falls.

Next: Tessa, on The Rules: the legal ideas an annual review must check, with a Two Systems comparison.
checklist: I produce six numbers on one page every year.
I convert everything into one reporting currency on one date.
My liquidity floor includes an allowance for guarantees being called.
I keep a guarantee register reconciled to the signed documents.
I calculate leverage both with and without guarantees.
I run concentration by asset, market and counterparty.
I compare every number with its written limit and with last year.
I record a decision for every breached limit.
head: Field checklist
speak: Mr Shabazz, net worth is the least useful number on your balance sheet. An annual review should produce six on one page. Net worth in the currency you spend. Liquidity coverage: cash and near-cash divided by a floor that includes an allowance for guarantees being called. Concentration: the largest exposure as a share of total assets. Leverage, both with and without guarantees, because a guarantee is a debt that has not arrived yet. Net currency exposure. And all-in cost, every fee as a share of the assets it serves. In the hypothetical example, net worth rose by a million dollars in a year while concentration climbed to 59 percent, guarantees rose and liquidity coverage fell below 1.0. The family got richer on paper and less safe in fact. Whichever number is closest to its limit is the binding constraint on the next commitment. A licensed adviser is required before I act.
terms: Liquidity coverage — usable liquid assets divided by the written liquidity floor.
Guarantee register — a list of every personal guarantee signed, with its amount, trigger, cap and expiry, reconciled to the documents.
All-in cost — the total of every fee paid across the structure, expressed as a share of the assets it serves.

hostile.q: Your net worth grew this year. Why should I worry about adding another guarantee?
hostile.a: Because my liquidity coverage is now below my own floor once the existing guarantees are counted, and my concentration is above my limit. Net worth rose mostly through a revaluation of illiquid project equity. Before I sign another guarantee I will restore liquidity above the floor, and I can show you the page with all six numbers and last year's figures beside them.

title: The Legal Checks Inside an Annual Review
summary: An annual review is also a legal check: does every protective structure still work, was every transfer made for genuine reasons at the right time, are trustees doing their duties, and do the estate documents match the assets where they actually sit? This lesson revisits the phase's hardest legal ideas, with a Two Systems comparison of Canada and Guyana.
body:
Most legal protection fails not because it was badly designed but because it was not maintained. The annual review is where you confirm that each structure still does what it was set up to do, and that nothing done this year has quietly undermined it.

Recall

Q. In Cole's Auditor's Chair last week, what was wrong with custody sitting with the manager's own affiliate?

A. It removed the one independent check. With no separate custodian statement, there is nothing to compare the manager's report against.

Q. In concept, how can a company owner be taxed differently on salary and on dividends?

A. Salary is usually deductible to the company and taxed as employment income, while dividends are paid from after-tax profit and taxed under separate rules. Verify the details against the primary source before you rely on them.

Q. What makes ring-fencing work in practice?

A. Real separation: separate bank accounts, separate records, proper capital, arm's-length dealings and no casual mixing of funds. A structure ignored in practice may be ignored by a court.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, the legal side of your wealth was designed in weeks 89 to 92. Design is the easy part. Each year you sign guarantees, move money, buy and sell, and sometimes change family circumstances. Any one of those can weaken a protection that was sound last year. The review is where you look for that damage while it is still repairable. Professional sign-off required: corporate lawyer and estate lawyer in each relevant jurisdiction.

Check one: timing and substance of transfers

In plain English: moving assets out of reach only protects them if it was done honestly, at a time when no claim was looming, and if you could still pay your debts afterwards. In week 89, Omar and Tessa called this the voidable transfer risk.

The professional framing is that courts in many systems can reverse a transfer made to defeat creditors, or one that left the transferor unable to meet known obligations, sometimes within fixed look-back periods. The tests, periods and remedies differ by jurisdiction; verify them against the primary source before you rely on them. The review therefore records, for every transfer into a protected layer this year, the date, the reason, the value and your solvency position at the time.

Worked example, hypothetical. In March a developer moved a 1,500,000 dollar investment account into a family holding structure, for a genuine estate-planning reason recorded by his lawyer. In June a project lender sent a covenant-breach notice that could lead to a guarantee call. The review should note both dates. The March transfer was made before the claim was foreseeable, with documented reasons, and he remained solvent afterwards. A transfer of the same account in July, after the notice, would look very different to a court. The same act, three months apart, can carry opposite legal weight.

Say that out loud now.

Protection put in early, for real reasons, holds. Protection put in under pressure invites reversal.

Check two: trusts are run, not just created

In week 90 Tessa taught that a trust separates legal ownership, held by the trustee, from benefit, held by the beneficiaries. A trustee owes duties: to act in the beneficiaries' interests, to follow the trust deed, to keep accounts, to avoid conflicts and to make decisions properly. If the trustee simply does what the settlor asks, a court may treat the trust as a sham or as the settlor's own property.

The review asks the trustee for this year's minutes, accounts and decisions. If there are none, the trust may not be working as designed. In week 91 we also met attribution concepts, where income from property given to certain family members may be taxed back to the person who gave it. The review notes any new gift or loan into a family structure so the tax adviser can check it. Verify those rules against the primary source before you rely on them.

A short hypothetical shows the difference. Trust A holds 2,000,000 dollars. Its trustee met twice this year, minuted a decision to make one distribution for a beneficiary's education after considering the deed, and kept accounts reviewed by an accountant. Trust B holds the same amount. Its trustee has no minutes, made three payments because the settlor phoned, and keeps no accounts. On paper both are trusts. Only one could show a court that it is run as one.

Check three: documents match the assets, where they sit

Land generally follows the law of the place where it is located, which lawyers call its situs. Company shares may follow the law of the place of incorporation. Bank accounts may be governed where the account is held. So the review maps each asset to its place and checks that a valid will, or confirmed advice, covers it there, and that no later document has accidentally revoked an earlier one.

Second worked example, hypothetical. This year the developer bought land in a second country. His existing will was drafted for his home country only, with a clause revoking all earlier wills. If he signs a separate will for the second country without care, the new will's standard revocation clause could revoke the home will. The fix is drafting each will to cover only its own assets and to leave the other in force. That is exactly the kind of interaction the review exists to catch. Professional sign-off required: estate lawyer in both jurisdictions.

Two Systems: Canada and Guyana

This is a conceptual comparison only. Verify every point against primary source before relying on it.

In Canada, wills, estates, trusts and property are mainly matters of provincial law, so the rules on formal validity, probate, intestate shares and dependants' claims can differ from province to province. Most provinces follow the common law tradition, while Quebec has a civil law system with its own rules for successions. Income tax at death is federal in concept and includes a rule that can treat assets as disposed of at death [unverified — confirm independently].

Guyana, as I understand it, moved from a Roman-Dutch legal heritage to English common law in the early twentieth century, and estates are proved through its court system with grants of probate or letters of administration [unverified — confirm independently]. Land in Guyana generally passes under Guyanese law and its own registration and transfer procedures, so a Canadian will alone may not be enough to deal with it [unverified — confirm independently]. The practical lesson is the same in both: identify where each asset sits, and get advice from a lawyer qualified there.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a protective structure that exists on paper and has been ignored in practice: an unminuted trust, a holding company used as a personal account, a transfer made after trouble began. The control is evidence. Each year, collect the minutes, accounts, transfer records and solvency notes that prove the structure is real.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner believes the structure protects him because a lawyer set it up. It protects him only as long as he respects it. The second mistake is moving assets in a hurry once a lender becomes difficult. That is the moment a transfer is most likely to be challenged.

Callback

In week 21, LEX taught piercing the corporate veil: courts can disregard a company where it is a mere façade or is used to evade existing obligations. Every check in today's lesson is the same idea applied to your personal structures. Separation earns respect from a court by being real, consistent and documented.

Recap

The review checks three legal things: that every transfer was timely, genuine and solvent; that trusts are being run by trustees doing their duties; and that the documents cover each asset under the law of the place where it sits. Canada and Guyana both reward the same discipline: local advice for local assets.

Next: Warrick, on The Numbers: a full annual review calculation, step by step.
checklist: I record the date, reason, value and my solvency for every transfer into a protected layer.
I never move assets in a hurry after a claim becomes foreseeable.
I collect trustee minutes, accounts and decisions every year.
I note every new gift or loan into a family structure for my tax adviser.
I map each asset to the place where it legally sits.
Each jurisdiction holding my assets is covered by a will or confirmed advice.
My wills are drafted so that one does not revoke another.
Professional sign-off from lawyers in each jurisdiction is on file.
head: Field checklist
speak: Mr Shabazz, legal protection usually fails through neglect, not bad design, so the annual review makes three legal checks. First, transfers: anything moved into a protected layer must have been moved early, for a genuine reason, while I could still pay my debts, because a transfer made after a claim was foreseeable invites reversal. I record the date, reason, value and solvency for each one. Second, trusts: a trustee must actually run the trust, with minutes, accounts and independent decisions, or a court may treat it as mine. Third, documents: each asset follows the law of the place where it sits, so each place needs a valid will or confirmed advice, drafted so one will does not revoke another. In Canada estates are mainly provincial; in Guyana land follows its own law and procedure. Verify both against primary source, and get sign-off from a lawyer in each jurisdiction.
terms: Voidable transfer — a transfer a court may reverse because it defeated creditors or left the transferor unable to pay known debts.
Sham trust — an arrangement that looks like a trust but in which the settlor in fact keeps control, so a court may disregard it.
Situs — the place where an asset is legally located, which often decides which law governs it.

hostile.q: You moved a large account into a family structure this year. How do I know it was not done to put it out of my reach?
hostile.a: Because the record shows it was done in March for an estate-planning reason documented by my lawyer at the time, months before any covenant issue arose, and that I remained solvent afterwards with my liquidity floor intact. I can provide the dated advice letter and a solvency statement as at the transfer date. I have moved nothing since your notice.

title: A Full Annual Review, Calculated Step by Step
summary: We run a complete hypothetical annual review: the balance sheet, the six numbers, a severe stress case with markets, currency and a guarantee call all at once, and then the size of the fix. The result shows a family that looks rich and comfortable until the stress case shows its liquidity would run out.
body:
The calculation that matters most in an annual review is the severe case: everything that tends to go wrong together, going wrong together. On paper our hypothetical family is worth 9,200,000. In the severe case it would be left with 65,000 of usable cash. The fix is small if you calculate it now.

Recall

Q. What are the five layers an annual review walks through?

A. Ownership layers, liquidity tiers, concentration, cost and conflicts, and protection and succession.

Q. Why should a liquidity floor include an allowance for guarantees?

A. Because a guarantee can be called at the worst moment and must be paid in cash. A floor that covers only living costs will fail on the day the guarantee is called.

Q. Why does the timing of a transfer into a protected structure matter?

A. Because a transfer made once a claim was foreseeable, or that left you unable to pay known debts, may be reversed. Early, genuine, solvent transfers are far more robust.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, the review page is only as good as the arithmetic under it. This is an odd week, so we work forward from the raw figures to the decision, showing every unit. All numbers are hypothetical round figures. Two currencies are involved: F, in which the development assets are valued, and H, the currency the family spends. Today 1 F buys 1.00 H.

Step 1. The balance sheet, in H

LineCurrencyValue in H
Project company sharesF6,000,000
Rental buildingF3,000,000
HomeH1,200,000
Investment account, independent custodianH900,000
CashH300,000
Rental mortgageFminus 1,800,000
Home mortgageHminus 400,000

Total assets are 6,000,000 plus 3,000,000 plus 1,200,000 plus 900,000 plus 300,000, which is 11,400,000 H. Total debt is 2,200,000 H. Net worth is 9,200,000 H. Off the balance sheet, the family has signed a 2,000,000 H guarantee on a construction loan. Annual spending is 150,000 H.

Step 2. The six numbers

Liquidity floor, by the family's written rule: 12 months of spending plus 20 percent of guarantees, which is 150,000 plus 400,000, or 550,000 H. Usable liquidity is cash plus the investment account, 1,200,000 H. Coverage is 1,200,000 divided by 550,000, about 2.18.

Concentration: project shares of 6,000,000 divided by 11,400,000 is about 52.6 percent, against a written limit of 50 percent. That is a breach.

Leverage: 2,200,000 divided by 11,400,000 is about 19.3 percent. With the guarantee, 4,200,000 divided by 11,400,000 is about 36.8 percent.

Currency: assets in F are 9,000,000 and debt in F is 1,800,000, so the net F position is 7,200,000, about 78 percent of net worth.

All-in cost: suppose fees across the structure total 55,000 H, about 0.6 percent of net worth and about 6.1 percent of the 900,000 investment account those managers touch.

Say that out loud now.

Coverage 2.18, concentration 52.6 percent, leverage 19 percent, 37 with the guarantee, 78 percent in a currency we do not spend.

Step 3. The severe case

The family's written severe case switches on everything at once: property in the F market falls 30 percent; currency F falls 20 percent, so 1 F buys 0.80 H; the investment account falls 15 percent; and the construction lender calls half the guarantee, 1,000,000 H.

Project shares: 6,000,000 F times 0.70 is 4,200,000 F, times 0.80 is 3,360,000 H. Rental building: 3,000,000 F times 0.70 is 2,100,000 F, times 0.80 is 1,680,000 H. Rental mortgage: still 1,800,000 F, times 0.80 is 1,440,000 H. Home unchanged at 1,200,000 H, home mortgage 400,000 H. Investment account: 900,000 times 0.85 is 765,000 H. Cash 300,000 H.

Assets before the call are 3,360,000 plus 1,680,000 plus 1,200,000 plus 765,000 plus 300,000, which is 7,305,000 H. Debts are 1,440,000 plus 400,000, which is 1,840,000 H. Net worth before the call is 5,465,000 H. The 1,000,000 call is paid from cash and investments: 300,000 plus 765,000 is 1,065,000, leaving 65,000 H. Net worth after the call is 4,465,000 H, down about 51 percent. Usable cash is 65,000 H, less than half a year of spending.

Step 4. Find the binding number

Net worth survives the severe case. Liquidity does not. A family worth over 4,000,000 in the severe case would be unable to pay a year's living costs without selling illiquid assets into a falling market. Liquidity is the binding constraint.

Step 5. Size the fix

The family wants 550,000 H of usable cash left after the severe case. Call the cash it should hold C, with the investment account kept at 900,000. After the case, usable liquidity is C plus 765,000 less the 1,000,000 call. Set that equal to 550,000: C plus 765,000 less 1,000,000 equals 550,000, so C equals 785,000 H. The family holds 300,000. The gap is 485,000 H.

Options include building the cash from project distributions, reducing the guarantee at the next loan negotiation, or reducing the concentrated position, which also cures the concentration breach. Each has a cost and a tax consequence, and a licensed adviser is required before you act.

Step 6. Test each fix in the same severe case

A fix is only proved when it is run back through the severe case. Take three options in turn.

Option A: raise cash to 785,000 H by retaining 485,000 of project distributions. In the severe case, cash plus investments are 785,000 plus 765,000, which is 1,550,000 H. After the 1,000,000 call, 550,000 H remains. The floor holds. Concentration is unchanged at about 52.6 percent before stress, so the breach remains to be dealt with separately.

Option B: negotiate the guarantee down to 1,000,000 H at the next loan, so the realistic call becomes 500,000 H. The floor itself falls to 150,000 plus 200,000, or 350,000 H. In the severe case, 1,065,000 less 500,000 leaves 565,000 H, above the new floor. This fix costs no cash, but it depends on a lender agreeing, which is a commercial negotiation, not a certainty.

Option C: sell 900,000 H of the project shares at today's value and hold the proceeds as cash. Concentration falls to 5,100,000 divided by 11,400,000, about 44.7 percent, curing the breach. In the severe case the remaining shares are worth 5,100,000 times 0.70 times 0.80, which is 2,856,000 H, and cash is 1,200,000. After the call, liquidity is 1,200,000 plus 765,000 less 1,000,000, which is 965,000 H. The floor holds with room to spare, and the currency exposure falls too. A sale may carry tax and transaction costs that must be subtracted first.

Option C solves two problems at once, which is often the sign of the right answer. It also gives up upside in the best-performing asset, which is why it is a decision for the family and not a formula.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is running the stress case on assets only and leaving the guarantee out. Without the call, this family looks comfortable in every case. The control is a written severe case that always includes the realistic guarantee call, taken from the guarantee register.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner stresses one variable at a time, a market fall here, a currency fall there, and finds each survivable. The severe case is defined by things happening together. Write it once, keep it fixed from year to year, and compare the results across years.

Callback

In week 44, Roman taught base, downside and severe cases for a project, with written triggers. This is the identical method on a family balance sheet, and the trigger is plain: when severe-case liquidity falls below the floor, the next commitment waits until the gap is closed.

Recap

Net worth 9,200,000 H, coverage 2.18 and a mild concentration breach looked fine. The severe case left 65,000 H of cash after a guarantee call. Holding 785,000 H rather than 300,000 closes the gap, and so would a smaller guarantee or a smaller concentrated position.

Next: Warrick, on The Room: a full mock annual wealth review meeting.
checklist: I build the balance sheet in one reporting currency, line by line.
I calculate all six review numbers with units.
My written severe case switches on market, currency, investments and a guarantee call together.
I take the guarantee call from my guarantee register.
I identify which number is the binding constraint.
I solve for the size of the fix rather than guessing it.
I keep the severe case fixed from year to year so results compare.
I act on the fix only with a licensed adviser.
head: Field checklist
speak: Mr Shabazz, in our hypothetical review the family is worth 9,200,000 H, with liquidity coverage of 2.18, concentration just above its 50 percent limit, leverage of 19 percent or 37 with the guarantee, and 78 percent of net worth in a currency it does not spend. Then the severe case: property down 30 percent, the currency down 20, investments down 15, and half the guarantee called at once. Net worth falls by about half, to 4,465,000 H, which survives. Usable cash falls to 65,000 H, which does not. Liquidity is the binding constraint. Solving for the fix, the family needs 785,000 H of cash, not 300,000, a gap of 485,000, or a smaller guarantee, or a smaller concentrated position. The lesson is to stress everything together and always include the guarantee call. A licensed adviser is required before I act.
terms: Severe case — a fixed, written stress scenario in which the risks that tend to move together all go wrong at once.
Binding constraint — the measure that fails first under stress and therefore limits the next decision.
Guarantee call — a lender's demand that a guarantor pay under a guarantee, usually in cash.

hostile.q: Your net worth is over nine million. Why can you not cover a one-million-dollar guarantee call?
hostile.a: I can cover it today. In my written severe case, where the market, the currency and my investments fall at the same time as the call, I would be left with too little cash for a year of living costs. That is why I am building cash by a stated amount from distributions before I sign anything new, and I can show you the calculation.

title: Mock Meeting: The Annual Wealth Review, Played in Full
summary: A full role-play of an annual wealth review. Warrick chairs; Tessa, Elias, Roman and Nadia attend; an outside investment manager presents. You run the agenda, hear a confident manager, a cautious tax adviser and an awkward estate finding, and close with recorded decisions.
body:
An annual wealth review is a meeting you chair, not one you attend. Your job is to keep it on the structure, make every adviser answer the question you asked, and leave with written decisions, each with an owner and a date.

Recall

Q. What was Rule 97?

A. I never close an annual review until my will, powers of attorney and beneficiary designations have been checked against the balance sheet I just built, updated where needed, and the location of every original recorded.

Q. What does a retirement income plan try to balance, in concept?

A. Spending needs, the order of withdrawals across differently taxed accounts, longevity and the risk of selling assets in a bad market. The tax rules are local; verify them against the primary source.

Q. What evidence helps a protective structure survive a challenge?

A. Dated reasons for each transfer, proof of solvency at the time, separate accounts and records, and minutes showing the structure was run as designed.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this is the full mock meeting for the checkpoint. Read it once, then play it aloud, taking your own lines. Everything here is hypothetical, and every adviser in the room is a role, not a recommendation. A licensed adviser is required before you act on any decision the meeting reaches.

The room and the agenda

Present: Warrick, as the family's wealth architect; Nadia, who prepared the consolidated statement; Roman, who ran the stress case; Elias, for tax; Tessa, for estate documents; and an outside investment manager who runs a 900,000 dollar account. The papers went out a week ago. The agenda, which you set: one, the six numbers against limits; two, the severe case; three, the investment account; four, tax calendar and changes; five, estate and insurance check; six, decisions.

Item one and two: you open

You: "Thank you all. We will take structure first and returns last. Nadia, please give us the six numbers against their limits, breaches only, in two minutes."

Nadia reports net worth of 9,200,000, coverage of 2.18, concentration of 52.6 percent against a 50 percent limit, and 78 percent of net worth in currency F. Roman then reports the severe case: 65,000 of usable cash after a guarantee call.

You: "So we have two findings. A concentration breach, and severe-case liquidity below the floor. We will decide both under item six. Questions on the numbers only, please."

Say that out loud now.

Structure first, returns last. Findings now, decisions under item six.

Item three: the manager

The manager opens with performance: a strong year, well ahead of his benchmark. You let him finish, then:

You: "Thank you. Three questions. Has the custodian changed? Do the custodian's year-end figures match yours? And what were your total fees, including fees inside any funds you used?"

He confirms the independent custodian, says the figures match, and gives a fee figure for his own charge only. You stay silent for two seconds. He adds the underlying fund fees. Nadia confirms the total, about 6 percent of the account including other advisers who touch it, which is the cost line from the six numbers.

You: "I am not deciding on your fees today. I would like a written comparison of the account's return after all fees with the benchmark after typical costs, by the end of the month."

Item four: tax

Elias reports that one holding structure may be affected by a rule change and that a deadline falls next quarter. He declines to give a conclusion until he has read the final text.

You: "Understood. What is the decision I will face, and by when?" He answers. You write it down. You do not ask him to guess.

Item five: the estate finding

Tessa reports that the will made for currency F's country names an executor who has moved abroad, and that a property bought this year in that country is not covered by any document.

You: "Thank you for finding that. That is exactly what this item is for. Please send me the options and a cost estimate this week, and I will sign whatever is needed before the end of the month. Rule 97 says this review does not close until it is done."

Tessa continues with insurance. The family's life cover was sized two years ago, before the 2,000,000 guarantee was signed, and the disability cover replaces only part of your income.

You: "Roman, if I died next month with that guarantee in force, what would the realistic call be, and would the current cover meet it alongside the family's floor?" Roman answers with the severe-case figure. The gap is visible in one sentence, and it becomes a sixth decision: a licensed insurance adviser to review cover against the guarantee register and report back within a month. You do not buy anything in the room. A review meeting finds gaps; it does not sell products.

Item six: decisions

You read each decision aloud, with an owner and date. One: retain 485,000 of distributions into cash, or reduce the project position, with Warrick to present both with tax effects from Elias within three weeks; you decide by a fixed date. Two: no new guarantee until severe-case liquidity is back above the floor. Three: manager to deliver the after-fee comparison by month end. Four: Tessa to deliver will options this week; signing before month end. Five: Nadia to circulate minutes within two days. Six: insurance cover reviewed against the guarantee register within a month.

The lines never to say

"Let's start with performance." It turns the meeting into a celebration and the structural findings get rushed.

"Just tell me what you would do." To the tax adviser, this invites a conclusion before the facts are confirmed.

"We can sort the will out next year." It is how the Hughes estate happened.

"Great year, everyone." Fine as a closing courtesy, wrong as an opening.

The question behind the question

When the manager leads with performance, the question behind it is whether you will judge him on returns alone. Answering with custody and fees tells him you will not. When Elias declines to conclude, the question behind it is whether you want comfort or accuracy. Taking the decision date instead of a guess tells him you want accuracy. When Tessa raises an awkward finding, the question behind it is whether bad news is welcome. Thanking her tells everyone in the room that it is.

When to stay silent and how to hold your state

Stay silent after each question to an adviser, and after the manager quotes his return. Keep your voice even when Tessa reports the gap in the documents; this is the review working, not failing. If you feel defensive about the concentration breach, remember that you set the limit and you are enforcing it. Slow down when you read the decisions aloud, because they are the only part of the meeting anyone will remember.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a review that ends with discussion and no decisions. The control is item six: every finding becomes a decision with an owner and a date, read aloud and minuted within two days.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner lets advisers set the agenda, so each presents his own area at length and nobody sees the whole. Set the agenda yourself, send it with the papers, and give each adviser a time limit.

Callback

In week 94, Warrick and Nadia taught the family office: an investment policy statement, consolidated reporting and managing advisers. Today's meeting is that system in motion. The policy sets the limits, the consolidated report shows the breaches, and the meeting turns them into decisions.

Recap

You chaired: structure first, findings before decisions, custody and fees before performance, a tax decision date rather than a guess, an estate gap fixed under Rule 97, and six decisions read aloud with owners and dates.

Next: Kema, on the Checkpoint: a mock interview and your recorded three-minute explanation.
checklist: I set and circulate the agenda with the papers in advance.
I take structure first and returns last.
I record findings first and make decisions under one final item.
I ask every manager about custody and total fees before performance.
I ask the tax adviser for the decision and its date, not a guess.
I thank whoever brings bad news.
I read every decision aloud with an owner and a date.
Minutes go out within two days.
head: Field checklist
speak: Mr Shabazz, in the mock annual review you chair, you do not attend. You set the agenda: six numbers against limits, the severe case, the investment account, tax, estate and insurance, then decisions. Structure first, returns last. Nadia reports a concentration breach and Roman reports severe-case liquidity below the floor; you note both for the final item. You ask the manager about custody, matching figures and total fees before discussing performance. You ask Elias for the decision and its date, not a guess. When Tessa finds a will gap, you thank her and invoke Rule 97: the review does not close until it is fixed. Then you read six decisions aloud, each with an owner and a date. Never open with performance, never ask an adviser to guess, never defer the will. Stay silent after hard questions, and slow down for the decisions. A licensed adviser is required before you act.
terms: Agenda control — the chair's setting of the order, time and scope of each item so the meeting serves its purpose.
Decision log — a dated record of each decision, its reason, its owner and its deadline.
After-fee return — an investment's return once every fee, including fees inside underlying funds, has been deducted.

hostile.q: I outperformed my benchmark by a wide margin this year. Why are we spending the meeting on custody and fees?
hostile.a: Because performance is measured after fees and on assets I can verify. I want to see the return after every fee against the benchmark after typical costs, and to confirm the custodian's figures match yours. If they do, the strong year speaks for itself. I am not judging you today; I am asking for the comparison by the end of the month.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Checkpoint: Wealth Architecture and Legacy, Under Questioning
summary: Kema's checkpoint for the wealth and legacy phase: a mock interview with a sceptical private banker, a three-minute recorded explanation scored on accuracy, structure, composure and the hard question, and the rules so far read aloud and restated in your own words.
body:
You have finished the phase when you can explain your whole wealth architecture to a sceptic in three minutes, answer the hardest question without notes, and state the rules you will not break in your own words.

Recall

Q. Name the six numbers an annual review produces.

A. Net worth in the reporting currency, liquidity coverage, concentration ratio, leverage with and without guarantees, net currency exposure, and all-in cost.

Q. In concept, what is the purpose of registered or tax-sheltered retirement accounts?

A. To encourage saving by deferring or exempting tax on growth, in exchange for limits on contributions and withdrawals. The rules are local; verify them against the primary source.

Q. Why does an asset protection plan need to be in place before trouble starts?

A. Because transfers made when claims are foreseeable can be challenged and reversed, while early, genuine and solvent arrangements are far more robust.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a checkpoint is not a quiz. It tests whether the ideas hold under pressure, spoken aloud, in front of someone who doubts you. Private bankers, lenders and future partners will each probe your personal structure, and the way you answer tells them whether the structure is real.

The mock interview

Kema plays a private banker considering you as a client and as a guarantor on a large construction loan. Answer each question aloud before you read the model.

Question 1. "Walk me through how your wealth is structured."

Model: "In three layers. Operating project companies carry development risk. A holding layer receives distributions. Personal and family assets sit apart from both, with liquidity in tiers. I measure it all in one reporting currency, against written limits."

Question 2. "How much could you put your hands on in a month?"

Model: "My tier 1 and tier 2 liquidity, which I can state, against a written floor of twelve months' spending plus a realistic allowance for guarantee calls. I report coverage as a ratio and I know my severe-case figure."

Question 3. "Most of your money is in one market. Why should that not worry me?"

Model: "It should be watched, and I watch it. I have a written concentration limit by asset, market and counterparty. When a revaluation took me over it this year, the review recorded a breach and a decision with a cure date."

Question 4. "Who holds your investments?"

Model: "An independent custodian that reports to me directly. No manager of mine also holds or values my assets. That is a rule, not a preference."

Question 5. "If you died next month, what happens to the projects you are guaranteeing?"

Model: "Current wills cover each jurisdiction where I hold assets, powers of attorney cover incapacity, each company has an alternate signing officer, and my insurance is being reviewed against my guarantee register. My executor knows where every original is."

Question 6, the hard question. "Your net worth went up this year. Your liquidity went down. Explain that."

Model: "Net worth rose through a revaluation of illiquid project equity, and I signed a new guarantee, which raised my liquidity floor. In my severe case, cash after a guarantee call would fall below the floor. So no new guarantee until I have restored it, and I have three options costed, including a partial sale that also cures the concentration breach."

Say that out loud now.

A follow-up the banker will try

A good sceptic does not stop at the first answer. Kema's follow-up: "You say you have three options. Which one will you choose, and why not just borrow against the project instead?"

Model: "I have not chosen yet, and I will not until the tax effect of each is known, because a sale can carry tax and transaction costs that change the comparison. I will not borrow against the project to fund liquidity, because that moves risk from the project layer into the personal layer and adds leverage to the exact position that is already too concentrated. Borrowing to buy safety is usually buying the opposite."

Notice what the model does. It refuses to guess, it names the missing fact, and it explains the refusal with a principle from the phase rather than a feeling.

The phase on one page

Before you record, hold the whole phase in one picture. Week 85 built the layers and liquidity tiers. Week 86 sized positions and personal leverage. Week 87 widened the view to other asset classes, correlation, fees and conflicts. Week 88 placed insurance against what would be owed. Week 89 taught asset protection and why timing matters. Weeks 90 and 91 built trusts, trustee duties and the tax concepts around them. Week 92 crossed borders with multiple wills and incapacity planning. Week 93 prepared heirs and separated fairness from equality. Week 94 ran the family office. Week 95 traced personal tax across a lifetime. Week 96 tested it all to failure, and this week inspected it in an annual review.

If one of those weeks feels thin, it will show in your recording. That is useful information, not a failure.

Record yourself

Now take your phone, open the voice recorder, and record a three-minute explanation of your wealth architecture to a sceptical private banker. Cover the layers, the six numbers, the severe case, custody and succession, and end by answering the hard question above. Do not read a script. Use, at most, five words on a card.

Then play it back and score yourself from 1 to 5 on each of four measures.

Accuracy. 5 means every concept was correct and no rate, threshold or legal conclusion was stated as fact. 1 means a material error.

Structure. 5 means bottom line first, three to five clear parts and a close. 1 means a list of thoughts in the order they arrived.

Composure. 5 means steady pace, deliberate pauses and no apology. 1 means rushing, filler words or defensiveness.

The hard question. 5 means you acknowledged the point, answered it with numbers and named the decision. 1 means you avoided it or argued with it.

A worked example of honest scoring. Suppose your recording gets the six numbers right but states a tax rate as if it were settled law. Accuracy is a 3, not a 4, because the error is exactly the kind a banker notices. Suppose you began with "So, basically, I have a lot of different things going on." Structure is a 2, however good the middle was. Score what was said, not what you meant.

Any score below 4 means re-record tomorrow, focusing only on that measure. Keep both recordings and note the date in your decision journal.

Rules I will not break

Read each rule below aloud, then restate it in your own words. If you cannot restate a rule without looking, read that week's Day 2 lesson again tonight. A rule you cannot say in your own words is a rule you will not use under pressure.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk at a checkpoint is grading yourself kindly. The recording is there so that you hear what a listener hears, not what you meant. The control is the rubric, applied strictly, and the rule that any score below 4 is re-recorded.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner memorises answers. A sceptic will change the question slightly and the memorised answer will fail. Learn the structure instead: layers, numbers, severe case, custody, succession. Any question about personal wealth lands somewhere in those five.

Callback

In week 9, the first checkpoint, you recorded yourself explaining the developer's job. Listen to that recording after this one if you still have it. In week 5, Kema taught bottom line first and the rule of three. Both should be audible now. The difference between the two recordings is the clearest measure of how far you have come.

Recap

The phase built wealth architecture: layers, liquidity, sizing, insurance, protection, trusts, cross-border estates, succession, the family office and personal tax, and then tested it with a post-mortem week and an annual review. The checkpoint asks you to say it under pressure, score it honestly and restate your rules.
